subtitle: Turn a behaviour described in words into states, a transition table and finally flip-flops and gates, then meet the silicon it runs on.

fsm.body: A vending machine is a perfect example of a state machine: it remembers how much money you have put in, and it reacts to the next coin accordingly. A finite state machine has a set of states, inputs, a next-state rule and outputs. In a Moore machine the output depends only on the state; in a Mealy machine on state and input, so it can react a clock earlier and may need fewer states. A state diagram draws states as circles and transitions as labelled arrows. In a Moore machine, the output depends on the current state alone.

In a Moore machine the output depends only on the state; in a Mealy machine it depends on state and input, so it can react a clock earlier and may need fewer states.
A state diagram draws states as circles and transitions as labelled arrows.

seq.body:
Let’s design one. Make a detector that raises its output when the input ends in 11. We need three states: q0 (no progress), q1 (last bit was a 1), q2 (saw 11). On input 1 move forward (q0→q1→q2, and q2 stays); on input 0 fall back to q0.

Test it. For 0110111 the final state is q2, so the machine accepts: yes. For 0101 the final state is q1, so no. Step through the string in the figure and see that the machine lives in q2 only after two 1s in a row. With overlapping detection, after seeing “111” the machine should be in q2, ready to fire on the next 1.
keynotes: A detector for input ending in 11 has states q0 (no progress), q1 (last bit was a 1) and q2 (saw 11).
On input 1 move forward (q0→q1→q2, and q2 stays); on input 0 fall back to q0.
It accepts 0110111 (final q2) and rejects 0101 (final q1).

design.body:
How do you go from a diagram to a real circuit? Follow a recipe, and it works every time. 1) Draw the state diagram. 2) Assign binary codes to states (n flip-flops for up to 2ⁿ states). 3) Write the state table: present state, input → next state, output. 4) Use each flip-flop’s excitation table to get input equations, and simplify them with K-maps. 5) Draw the circuit and check unused states go somewhere safe.

Each step refines the previous one, as the figure shows. How many flip-flops do you need? A machine with 5 states needs ⌈log₂ 5⌉ = 3, since 2² = 4 < 5 ≤ 8 = 2³. A 9-state machine needs four.
keynotes: Recipe: draw the state diagram, assign binary codes to states, write the state table, use excitation tables and K-maps for the input equations, then draw the circuit and check unused states.
n flip-flops cover up to 2ⁿ states.
A machine with 5 states needs ⌈log₂ 5⌉ = 3 flip-flops.

ttl.body:
Gates are physical things made of transistors, and different technologies give different trade-offs. You will meet them in every datasheet you read. Gates are built in families. TTL (bipolar, 5 V) is fast but power-hungry; CMOS (complementary MOSFETs) uses almost no power except when switching and is the basis of all modern chips.

The key figures to compare are propagation delay (how long an output takes to change), power dissipation, noise margin (NM = VIH − VOH style gap between output and input thresholds) and fan-out (how many inputs one output can drive). Suppose a gate outputs at least 4.0 V for a 1 and the next gate accepts any input ≥ 3.5 V as 1. The high-level noise margin = V_OH(min) − V_IH(min) = 4.0 − 3.5 = 0.5 V. A larger noise margin means the circuit tolerates more noise.
keynotes: TTL (bipolar, 5 V) is fast but power-hungry; CMOS uses almost no power except when switching and is the basis of all modern chips.
Key figures are propagation delay, power dissipation, noise margin and fan-out (how many inputs one output can drive).
A gate outputting at least 4.0 V for a 1 into an input needing 3.5 V has a high-level noise margin of 0.5 V.

cmos.body:
Look inside a CMOS inverter and you find two switches working as a team. A CMOS inverter is a PMOS (pull-up to VDD) over an NMOS (pull-down to ground) sharing gate and output: input 0 turns the PMOS on, output 1; input 1 turns the NMOS on, output 0. With input 0 the PMOS connects the output to VDD, as the figure shows.

Only one conducts in steady state, so static power is near zero; power is spent charging and discharging load capacitance: P = C·V²·f. A NAND puts two NMOS in series and two PMOS in parallel. Try C = 10 pF, V = 3.3 V, f = 50 MHz: dynamic power P = C V² f = 10 pF · 3.3² · 50 MHz = 5.4 mW. CMOS uses almost no static power because one of the two transistors is always off.
keynotes: A CMOS inverter is a PMOS (pull-up to VDD) over an NMOS (pull-down to ground) sharing gate and output.
Only one conducts in steady state, so static power is near zero; power is spent charging load capacitance: P = C·V²·f.
With C = 10 pF, V = 3.3 V and f = 50 MHz, P = 5.4 mW; a NAND puts two NMOS in series and two PMOS in parallel.

mem.body:
Instead of wiring gates by hand, what if you could load a configuration into a chip? That is programmable logic. A ROM is a look-up table (2ⁿ words of m bits implement any m functions of n inputs); a PLA/PAL programs AND and OR planes; an FPGA has thousands of small look-up tables and flip-flops joined by programmable routing.

A 4-input look-up table stores one output bit for each input pattern, 2⁴ = 16 bits. Memory comes in two kinds too: SRAM (flip-flop cell, fast, 6 transistors) and DRAM (capacitor, dense, refreshed). A 6-input LUT can implement any function of six inputs.
keynotes: A ROM is a look-up table: 2ⁿ words of m bits implement any m functions of n inputs.
A PLA/PAL programs AND and OR planes; an FPGA has thousands of small look-up tables and flip-flops joined by programmable routing.
A 4-input look-up table stores 2⁴ = 16 bits; SRAM (6 transistors, fast) differs from DRAM (capacitor, dense, refreshed).
